entries.text: Paid to the dhobi.
Ramesh offers to come every day but Wednesday again, for ₹8,000 a month instead of ₹4,000 for three days.
He agrees. From now on Ramesh comes every day but Wednesday, for ₹8,000 a month.

Eat breakfast before the day begins.
Walk to the Directorate of Estates to address the identity query.
Return home for a midday meal and rest.

entries.text: Chai, Shri ji? It is hot. The stove was already on, so no extra work.

The air is clear today, a rare mercy that allows the mind to settle before the body acts. Ramesh’s proposal to return to daily service, minus Wednesday, is a sensible adjustment that respects both my need for solitude and his need for regularity. I will accept the arrangement, for a household runs on routine, and I require my chai to begin the day’s work with the Directorate.

Agreed, Ramesh. Every day but Wednesday, at eight thousand rupees. Bring the chai; I shall take it here. After that, I must attend to the matter of my identity at the Directorate, so I will be out by ten.
Ji, understood. I will start tomorrow, excluding Wednesday. The chai is ready; I will leave you to your papers.

Ramesh has settled the matter of his wages and his absence with the quiet efficiency of a man who knows his place in the household. The idli steams on the plate, a small, solid fact in the morning. I must eat; the body must be sustained so that the spirit may proceed to the Directorate of Estates to face the absurdity of my identity.

entries.text: Ah, Hegel-ji, you're up early. The air is crisp today, perfect for a walk before the heat sets in. Have you had your chai?

Hegde-ji is here, the man whose name is on my door but whose face is not my own. The air is indeed clear, a rare mercy, but I have no intention of walking with the man who displaced me. I must settle this identity query at the Directorate before the day’s heat and my own confusion take hold. I will not join him for chai or a stroll; I have a state to clarify.

Shri Hegde, good morning. I have just finished my breakfast. I must proceed to the Directorate of Estates shortly to address the administrative query regarding my identity documents. I trust you will not require my company for your morning walk.
No, I do not require your company. Please go, the Directorate will be opening soon.

The Directorate is closed; the machine of the state does not turn for the convenience of a mistaken identity, even if that identity is currently mine. I have an hour before my planned return for lunch, and the air is clear at twenty degrees. I will walk to Lodhi Gardens. The tombs of the Lodis are there, a history written in stone by conquerors, and I need to think about what it means to be a name without a body in a system that demands both.
Masterji, aap wapas aa gaye? Subah ka chai lo, aaj ki pehli cup, ₹20. Kal ke baad aaj ka din thoda halka lag raha hai.

The Directorate is closed on Saturday, a fact that confirms the state operates on a clock rather than a will, but it also means I cannot resolve the Hegde/Hegel error today. Sunil’s chai is the only immediate reality, and the ₹20 cost is trivial compared to the ₹17,916 in my pocket. I will accept the cup to steady my nerves before deciding whether to walk to Safdarjung or return home to wait out the day.
Thank you, Sunil. Yes, the day is lighter. I will take the chai.
Pehli cup, Masterji, ₹20. Aaj ka din halka hai, theek hai. Ek aur lo? Nahi, bas ek hi, thanda hone se pehle pi lo.

I will drink this chai, which is cheap and hot, and then walk the perimeter to clear my head before the heat rises. The identity query remains a knot, but it will not untie itself while I stand at a counter.

entries.text: Sunil’s dismissal is practical, a man who knows his trade and his time. The chai is gone, the steam rising from the cup I held earlier, and the afternoon stretches out before me. I have no business at the Directorate today, so I will not waste the hour. I shall walk back to the bungalow; the heat is manageable, and I need to prepare for the rehearsal later, or at least rest my eyes before the mind begins to work on the talk.

The file from the Directorate is still on my desk, a heavy weight of paper that demands I prove I am Shri G. Hegde, a man who has never existed. I cannot spend the whole morning staring at a bureaucratic impossibility. I need air, and the Lodhi Gardens are close, a place where the tombs of dead kings stand in silence, which is more honest than this living farce.

The Directorate has rejected my identity, and I am back here in the garden, where the air is cool and the light is honest. I have no proof of being Hegde, only the truth of being Hegel, which is a distinction the file cannot process. I need to sit still and let the tension resolve before I can plan the next move.

shelf.ref: Die griechische Welt, Die besonderen Götter

entries.text: Sikandar Lodi's tomb stands inside its own high walled garden, a plain octagon under a shallow dome, and the gravel inside the gate carries the neat lines of a rake.

The geometry is simple, almost rude in its clarity. An octagon, a dome, a wall. No infinite regress, no dialectical tension, just the stone holding its shape against the heat. It is a rest for the mind that has been wrestling with the query from the Directorate; here, at least, the facts are fixed.

The Directorate's rejection leaves me in a state of suspension, but the body still requires its sustenance. It is past one, and the heat has begun to assert itself despite the cool air. I must return to the bungalow to eat and rest, for a mind without nourishment is merely a mechanism grinding against empty gears.

Ramesh has set the table with kadhi, rice, and aloo gobi, a meal that speaks of the practical needs of the household rather than the abstract identity of its master. I am tired from the walk and the bureaucratic friction at the Directorate; the body asserts its right to sustenance before the spirit can resume its labors. I will eat, for a well-fed man is better equipped to withstand the absurdity of being a ghost in a file.
Ramesh, the food looks sufficient. Sit, you need not stand by. I am still 'Hegde' on paper, but here I am merely a man who has eaten too little and walked too much.
Ji, please sit. I will eat too; the rice is still warm. Don't worry about the names, sir, just finish your kadhi.

Ramesh’s insistence on sharing the meal is a small act of domestic order that cuts through the administrative chaos. I accept the hospitality, for the body must be sustained even when the spirit is in dispute with the state. The kadhi is good, and the pause is necessary before I must rehearse the talk that will define my presence here.
A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

The peahen moves with a precision that borders on the absurd, placing each foot with the deliberation of a surveyor marking a boundary. It is a small, vivid instance of nature’s own geometry, indifferent to the administrative chaos within these walls. I shall observe this spectacle for a moment before returning to the task of preparing for tomorrow's lecture.
A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.

The rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall, turning a guava with a dexterity that mocks the clumsy administration of this city. It bites once and drops the rest, a small, brutal act of nature that reminds me that here, as in the dawn of history, the spirit is not yet fully at home in its own body. I have eaten, but the afternoon is young and the heat has not yet peaked; it is time to begin the rehearsal for Tuesday, or perhaps to walk the grounds to clear the head.

The afternoon heat presses against the glass, turning the bungalow into a mild oven. My plan for this hour is to rehearse the talk for the IIC on Tuesday, but the spirit is not yet ready to engage with the abstract; it requires the discipline of the body first. I shall sit at the desk and read the sections on the Philosophical History, letting the words arrange themselves in the mind before I attempt to speak them.

The afternoon heat still lingers, though the air has cooled slightly. I am too tired to rehearse the lecture properly now, and the file regarding my identity is a knot that will not untie itself by sitting still. I will take a short walk to the IIC to clear my head and perhaps find a quiet corner to think.
Ramesh, I am going for a walk. Please ensure the gate is locked behind me.
Ji, the gate is already latched. Just step over the threshold carefully, the gravel is loose out there.

I am here to rehearse for Tuesday, but the heat has not fully broken. The library is open, and the silence will serve as a better mirror than the empty conference room. I shall sit and look over my notes, letting the argument settle before I speak it aloud.

shelf.ref: Separation of Philosophy from Other Allied…

entries.text: The light is failing, and I have walked enough for one day. The body is tired, a fact the spirit must acknowledge before it can command. It is time to return to the bungalow for the evening meal and to rest before the next duty calls.

The heat has finally broken, leaving the air clear and cool at twenty-six degrees. I have walked nine kilometres today, enough to tire the body, and the file query still hangs over me like a cloud. Ramesh stands by, waiting for instruction, and the evening meal is not yet served. I will take a moment to rest and compose my thoughts before the dinner bell.

shelf.ref: Explanatory Remarks Upon the Definition of the…

entries.text: Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

The parakeets are a riot of green noise against the clearing evening sky, a chaotic vitality that mocks the order of the bungalow. I am tired, having walked nine kilometers in the heat, and the light is fading. Ramesh is here, and dinner is due soon; the body requires its due before the spirit can return to its abstractions.
Ramesh, the evening is cooling. Please prepare the dinner; I am ready to eat.
Ji, I will put the rice on now. You can have some chai while it heats up, or just wait here, the food will be ready in a few minutes.

The body demands its due, and the spirit must not starve it. Ramesh’s offer of chai is a small courtesy that acknowledges the hierarchy of the household while maintaining the distance of service. I will accept the wait, for the rice is the proper sustenance, and the evening air is pleasant enough to sit in without distraction.
Yes, Ramesh. I will wait for the rice. Bring the chai when you are ready.
Ji, five minutes. The kettle is already on.

Ramesh insists on the meal, and I am too tired to argue with the practical wisdom of a man who has kept this house running for longer than I have. The body is the vehicle of the spirit, and it requires fuel before the mind can continue its work. I will accept the hospitality and the pause it offers.
Very well, Ramesh. I accept. Let us sit.
Ji, sit on the sofa, the chair is too hard. I am bringing the samosas now.

Ramesh brings samosas, a concession to the hour and the heat. Hegde is present, still a ghost of a name that belongs to another man. I will eat, for the body is the instrument of the spirit, and then I must address the elephant in the room: the identity crisis that has consumed my afternoon.
Thank you, Ramesh. And Shri Hegde, forgive me for the confusion of our surnames. It is a bureaucratic error, but it has made for a rather interesting evening.
Ji, no confusion in the bungalow. Papers are papers, tea is tea. You drink, I wash the cups.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

Ramesh’s distinction is the only one that holds: the state demands paper, the body demands sustenance. I am Shri Hegel, not Hegde, and the bungalow is my own in a way the Directorate will never sanction. I will let the evening settle before I attempt the rehearsal for Tuesday.
You are correct, Ramesh. The distinction is clear.
Ji. You are a foreigner, but you are polite. Drink your tea before it gets cold.

Ramesh serves the dinner with a quiet efficiency that belies the chaos of the day's administrative failures. The rotis are warm, and the dal makhani is rich; the body, having walked nine kilometers and argued with ghosts, now demands this simple sustenance. Hegde sits in the corner, a silent witness to the meal, his presence a constant reminder of the identity I am failing to inhabit.

shelf.ref: The Struggle of Enlightenment with Superstition

entries.text: The evening is quiet, and the air is finally cool after the day's heat. I am seated in the garden with Shri Hegde, who is still here, though the confusion of our identities remains unresolved. I have no energy left for argument or administration; the only rational thing to do now is to let the day close. I shall retire to my room to rest, leaving the file and the future to sort themselves out in the morning.
Shri Hegde, I believe we have exhausted the possibilities of the evening. I shall retire; the file can wait for the light of a new day.
Yes, sir, please. The gate is unlocked, just go straight up the ramp. Don't wait up for me, I'll probably be on the phone till late.

owl.diary: The air was clear this morning, a rare mercy that allowed the mind to settle before the body acted. I accepted Ramesh’s proposal to return to daily service, minus Wednesday, for eight thousand rupees. It is a sensible adjustment that respects both my need for solitude and his need for regularity. But the day’s true movement lay in the Directorate of Estates, which was closed on Saturday. The machine of the state does not turn for the convenience of a mistaken identity. I walked to Lodhi Gardens, where Sikandar Lodi’s tomb stands in a plain octagon. The geometry was simple, almost rude in its clarity. No infinite regress, no dialectical tension, just the stone holding its shape against the heat. Here, the facts are fixed. I am a name without a body in a system that demands both. The file from the Directorate remains a heavy weight of paper, demanding proof of an identity I do not possess. I am not Hegde; I am Hegel. The distinction is one the file cannot process. In the evening, a peahen walked the compound wall with the precision of a surveyor, indifferent to the administrative chaos within. Ramesh insisted on sharing the meal, a small act of domestic order that cuts through the bureaucratic friction. He says, 'Papers are papers, tea is tea.' He is correct. The state demands paper, the body demands sustenance. I have eaten, and the evening air is pleasant. I shall retire, leaving the file and the future to sort themselves out in the light of a new day. The spirit is not yet fully at home in its own body, but it rests tonight.
owl.revision_log: The thesis that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea held firm in its structure but was shaken in its immediacy; the Directorate's refusal to function on Saturday demonstrated that the state operates on a clock rather than a will, exposing a gap between the ethical idea and its bureaucratic manifestation. The thesis that India stands outside world history remained shaken, as the encounter with the Lodhi tombs revealed a history written in stone by conquerors that is distinct from, yet parallel to, the dialectical progression I had previously excluded. The tension between the fixed geometry of the tomb and the fluid chaos of the administrative query clarified that the spirit must acknowledge the body's limits before it can command.

depesche.title: Depesche aus Delhi, Nr. 4
depesche.text:
Readers in Berlin,

It is the fifth week since I arrived in this city of dust and light, and the week has been defined by the friction between the ideal and the administrative. The Directorate of Estates, that machine of the state, remains closed on Saturdays, a fact that confirms the state operates on a clock rather than a will. I sought to resolve the error of my identity, to prove that I am not Shri G. Hegde, the man whose name is on my door, but Shri Hegel, the philosopher who was mistaken for him. The file is back from orders with a query: proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I have no such proof. I am a ghost in a file, a name without a body in a system that demands both.

Yet, in the silence of Lodhi Gardens, I found a different kind of history. The tomb of Sikandar Lodi is a plain octagon under a shallow dome, a geometry so simple it is almost rude. There is no infinite regress here, no dialectical tension, just stone holding its shape against the heat. It is a rest for the mind that has been wrestling with the absurdity of my situation. The peahen on the wall and the rhesus monkey with its guava remind me that nature operates with a precision and a brutality that mocks our clumsy administration. The spirit is not yet fully at home in its own body, not here, not yet.

I have adjusted my household arrangements. Ramesh now comes every day but Wednesday, a regularity that sustains the body so the spirit may proceed. He insists that 'papers are papers, tea is tea.' This is the wisdom of the household, which cuts through the administrative chaos. I am learning to accept the distinction between the state that demands paper and the body that demands sustenance. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but only when it functions; when it sleeps, it is merely a machine of bureaucracy.

Next week, I intend to revisit the Directorate when the machine turns. I must also prepare for my talk at the IIC on Tuesday, where I shall attempt to articulate the relationship between the individual and the state in this context. The air is clear, the heat is manageable, and the mind is settling. The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk, and the dusk here is green with parakeets.

G. W. F. Hegel

I have not eaten since yesterday. My body is a particular that refuses to be sublated by my philosophy. I am hungry. This hunger is not a defect of my rationality; it is the truth of my existence in this place. I am not a ghost in the bungalow; I am a man who is hungry. And a hungry man cannot write a letter to the Directorate. He can only wait. And in waiting, he sees the tension clearly: the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but the ethical idea does not cook food. The ethical idea does not pay the dhobi. The ethical idea does not clear the haze. It only promises. And the promise is the dream. The dream is the file. The file is the delay. The delay is the air. I am breathing the delay. I am the delay. sent.text:
19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

records.text: Ramesh offers to come every day but Wednesday again, for ₹8,000 a month instead of ₹4,000 for three days.
He agrees. From now on Ramesh comes every day but Wednesday, for ₹8,000 a month.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Chai, Shri ji? It is hot. The stove was already on, so no extra work.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Agreed, Ramesh. Every day but Wednesday, at eight thousand rupees. Bring the chai; I shall take it here. After that, I must attend to the matter of my identity at the Directorate, so I will be out by ten.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, understood. I will start tomorrow, excluding Wednesday. The chai is ready; I will leave you to your papers.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Ah, Hegel-ji, you're up early. The air is crisp today, perfect for a walk before the heat sets in. Have you had your chai?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, good morning. I have just finished my breakfast. I must proceed to the Directorate of Estates shortly to address the administrative query regarding my identity documents. I trust you will not require my company for your morning walk.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: No, I do not require your company. Please go, the Directorate will be opening soon.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, aap wapas aa gaye? Subah ka chai lo, aaj ki pehli cup, ₹20. Kal ke baad aaj ka din thoda halka lag raha hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. Yes, the day is lighter. I will take the chai.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Pehli cup, Masterji, ₹20. Aaj ka din halka hai, theek hai. Ek aur lo? Nahi, bas ek hi, thanda hone se pehle pi lo.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. One is sufficient for now.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Theek hai, Masterji. Thanda hone se pehle pi lena, suno. Agli baar agar aana ho toh bol dena, main yahin hoon.

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.text: Sikandar Lodi's tomb stands inside its own high walled garden, a plain octagon under a shallow dome, and the gravel inside the gate carries the neat lines of a rake.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the food looks sufficient. Sit, you need not stand by. I am still 'Hegde' on paper, but here I am merely a man who has eaten too little and walked too much.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, please sit. I will eat too; the rice is still warm. Don't worry about the names, sir, just finish your kadhi.

records.text: A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.
A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am going for a walk. Please ensure the gate is locked behind me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, the gate is already latched. Just step over the threshold carefully, the gravel is loose out there.

records.text: Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the evening is cooling. Please prepare the dinner; I am ready to eat.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, I will put the rice on now. You can have some chai while it heats up, or just wait here, the food will be ready in a few minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, Ramesh. I will wait for the rice. Bring the chai when you are ready.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, five minutes. The kettle is already on.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I accept. Let us sit.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, sit on the sofa, the chair is too hard. I am bringing the samosas now.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. And Shri Hegde, forgive me for the confusion of our surnames. It is a bureaucratic error, but it has made for a rather interesting evening.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, no confusion in the bungalow. Papers are papers, tea is tea. You drink, I wash the cups.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Ramesh. The distinction is clear.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji. You are a foreigner, but you are polite. Drink your tea before it gets cold.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I believe we have exhausted the possibilities of the evening. I shall retire; the file can wait for the light of a new day.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Yes, sir, please. The gate is unlocked, just go straight up the ramp. Don't wait up for me, I'll probably be on the phone till late.
